idiom_name: Proc/lambda stored by the context (hash of lambdas as the strategy registry)
implementation_notes: Ruby expresses a strategy as a callable object: a block captured with &block (or yielded), a Proc created by Kernel#lambda / ->(), or a Method object obtained with method(:name), all invoked with #call (aliases [] and ===). Enumerable#sort_by, map(&:sym) and min_by show the standard library taking strategy-like callables everywhere, and the idiomatic registry is a frozen hash of lambdas indexed with fetch, which raises on an unknown key instead of silently returning nil. Prefer a lambda for strategies: it enforces arity and returns from itself, while a proc ignores extra arguments and returns from the enclosing method. The class-per-strategy form is still justified when the algorithm carries state or offers several operations.
pitfalls: Proc semantics differ from lambda: a proc ignores extra arguments and returns from the method that created it, so a strategy stored as a proc can unexpectedly unwind its creator's stack - use ->() lambdas for strategies.
A block is not an object until it is captured: a method that yields without requiring a block raises LocalJumpError only when the missing strategy is used, so validate at construction time.
A Method object (method(:price)) carries its receiver, so using it as a strategy keeps that object alive and shares its state across every context that holds the method.
